query: What factors are reported to contribute to the development of coronary artery disease?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- Atherosclerotic plaque accumulation in the coronary arteries is the leading cause of coronary heart disease, also known as coronary artery disease. Plaque causes coronary arteries to harden and narrow, potentially reducing or blocking blood flow to the heart muscle. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0027; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/coronary-heart-disease/causes]
- CDC directly states that coronary artery disease can weaken heart muscle over time and may lead to heart failure. The Causes section explains that atherosclerotic plaque narrows coronary arteries and may partially or completely obstruct blood flow. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0031; https://www.cdc.gov/heart-disease/about/coronary-artery-disease.html]
- NHLBI identifies plaque accumulation in major surface coronary arteries as a leading cause of coronary heart disease, and describes narrowing of arteries. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0001; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/coronary-heart-disease/causes]
- NHLBI lists coronary heart disease or prior heart attack among conditions that can damage heart muscle and cause HFrEF. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0003; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart-failure/causes]
- NHLBI states that chronic conditions damaging or weakening heart muscle are major causes of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. In HFrEF the weakened left ventricle cannot pump sufficient blood. Coronary heart disease and myocardial infarction are identified as conditions that can deprive heart muscle of adequate oxygen and contribute to this outcome. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0033; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart-failure/causes]

query: What factors are reported to contribute to the development of type 2 diabetes?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- NIDDK lists limited physical activity among reported risk factors for type 2 diabetes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0006; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/risk-factors-type-2-diabetes]
- NIDDK includes family history in its list of type 2 diabetes risk factors. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0007; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/risk-factors-type-2-diabetes]
- NIDDK states that type 2 diabetes develops when the body has difficulty using insulin and the pancreas does not make enough insulin to maintain glucose balance. Insulin resistance contributes to hyperglycemia and type 2 diabetes in the context of inadequate insulin secretion. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0036; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes]
- NIDDK lists overweight or obesity among circumstances associated with higher likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0005; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/risk-factors-type-2-diabetes]
- Endotext describes insulin resistance in liver and muscle as an important pathogenic feature of type 2 diabetes; compensatory beta-cell secretion can initially maintain normal glucose, whereas inadequate beta-cell compensation permits hyperglycemia and progression to overt diabetes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0037; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279115/]

query: What factors are reported to contribute to the development of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- Wechsler and Wells describe cigarette smoke exposure as an inflammatory trigger in COPD. Chronic smoking increases oxidative stress, which contributes to lung inflammation. Smoke-related epithelial signaling releases cytokines and chemokines that recruit inflammatory cells, including neutrophils and macrophages, sustaining airway inflammatory responses. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0044; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11417604/]
- The review explains that inflammatory processes contribute to mucus hypersecretion, goblet cell hyperplasia, airway remodeling and small-airway fibrosis. These pathological changes, together with epithelial and mucociliary dysfunction, increase airway resistance, air trapping and persistent airflow obstruction in COPD. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0045; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11417604/]

query: What factors are reported to contribute to the development of depression?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- Li et al. synthesized 34 prospective cohort studies involving 172077 participants and reported an increased risk of subsequent depression among individuals with insomnia. The pooled relative risk was 2.27 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.89 to 2.71. Eligible depression outcomes included self-reported depressive symptom scales, clinician diagnoses and structured diagnostic interviews. These findings establish insomnia as a prospective predictor of subsequent depressive outcomes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0069; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27816065/]
- MedlinePlus describes higher depression risk when close relatives have depression or another mental health disorder. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0019; https://medlineplus.gov/depression.html]
- MedlinePlus describes trauma and stressful life events as factors that may raise risk for depression. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0020; https://medlineplus.gov/depression.html]
- Alvaro et al. reviewed nine independent studies, including eight longitudinal studies, examining sleep disturbances and depression or anxiety. Several studies found that insomnia or sleep problems predicted later depression or higher depression levels, while other analyses identified reverse or bidirectional relationships. The review supports a longitudinal association between insomnia or sleep disruption and later depressive outcomes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0068; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3669059/]

query: Which underlying conditions or exposures might be involved in the onset of coronary artery disease?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- Atherosclerotic plaque accumulation in the coronary arteries is the leading cause of coronary heart disease, also known as coronary artery disease. Plaque causes coronary arteries to harden and narrow, potentially reducing or blocking blood flow to the heart muscle. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0027; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/coronary-heart-disease/causes]
- CDC directly states that coronary artery disease can weaken heart muscle over time and may lead to heart failure. The Causes section explains that atherosclerotic plaque narrows coronary arteries and may partially or completely obstruct blood flow. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0031; https://www.cdc.gov/heart-disease/about/coronary-artery-disease.html]
- NHLBI lists coronary heart disease or prior heart attack among conditions that can damage heart muscle and cause HFrEF. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0003; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart-failure/causes]
- NHLBI identifies plaque accumulation in major surface coronary arteries as a leading cause of coronary heart disease, and describes narrowing of arteries. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0001; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/coronary-heart-disease/causes]
- NHLBI states that chronic conditions damaging or weakening heart muscle are major causes of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. In HFrEF the weakened left ventricle cannot pump sufficient blood. Coronary heart disease and myocardial infarction are identified as conditions that can deprive heart muscle of adequate oxygen and contribute to this outcome. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0033; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart-failure/causes]

query: Which underlying conditions or exposures might be involved in the onset of tuberculosis?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- Ravimohan et al. describe pulmonary tuberculosis producing destructive lung pathology through caseous necrosis, cavitation and abnormal tissue repair. Caseation destroys alveolar structures and neighbouring tissue, while subsequent healing can produce fibrosis and architectural distortion. Host inflammatory responses and matrix-degrading proteases are implicated in these processes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0058; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6019552/]
- Meghji et al. describe post-tuberculosis lung disease as encompassing residual parenchymal and airway abnormalities, including fibrosis, cavitation and bronchiectasis, alongside persistent respiratory symptoms and impaired lung function. The review reports ongoing abnormalities after completion of TB treatment and recognizes an association between residual structural pathology and post-TB respiratory limitation. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0060; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7618543/]

query: Which underlying conditions or exposures might be involved in the onset of depression?

- MedlinePlus describes higher depression risk when close relatives have depression or another mental health disorder. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0019; https://medlineplus.gov/depression.html]

- Alvaro et al. reviewed nine independent studies, including eight longitudinal studies, examining sleep disturbances and depression or anxiety. Several studies found that insomnia or sleep problems predicted later depression or higher depression levels, while other analyses identified reverse or bidirectional relationships. The review supports a longitudinal association between insomnia or sleep disruption and later depressive outcomes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0068; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3669059/]

Eligible depression outcomes included self-reported depressive symptom scales, clinician diagnoses and structured diagnostic interviews. These findings establish insomnia as a prospective predictor of subsequent depressive outcomes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0069; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27816065/]

query: Which condition affecting the coronary arteries should be investigated when assessing narrowed blood supply to heart muscle?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- Atherosclerotic plaque accumulation in the coronary arteries is the leading cause of coronary heart disease, also known as coronary artery disease. Plaque causes coronary arteries to harden and narrow, potentially reducing or blocking blood flow to the heart muscle. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0027; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/coronary-heart-disease/causes]
- CDC directly states that coronary artery disease can weaken heart muscle over time and may lead to heart failure. The Causes section explains that atherosclerotic plaque narrows coronary arteries and may partially or completely obstruct blood flow. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0031; https://www.cdc.gov/heart-disease/about/coronary-artery-disease.html]
- AHA explains that coronary atherosclerotic plaque can narrow arteries or rupture and produce a clot that blocks myocardial blood flow. Prolonged interruption of blood flow causes heart muscle injury or death. Damaged muscle may heal with scar tissue and leave the heart weakened with reduced pumping function. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0032; https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/heart-attack/about-heart-attacks]

- NIDDK defines diabetic kidney disease as kidney disease caused by diabetes. It explains that high glucose can damage renal blood vessels and impair their function, while kidney damage can reduce filtration of blood and allow waste to accumulate. - NIDDK directly states that elevated blood glucose can damage kidney filters. Kidney disease caused by diabetes is identified as diabetic kidney disease. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0040; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK explains that high blood pressure can narrow and damage renal blood vessels and reduce blood flow. Damaged renal vessels may no longer function properly, impairing the kidneys' ability to remove waste and excess fluid. The article also identifies hypertension as a cause of kidney disease and describes progressive damage that can lead to kidney failure. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0048; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/high-blood-pressure]

- NIDDK states that hypertension can damage renal blood vessels and other components of the kidney filtering system. Damage to these structures can impair the kidneys' ability to remove waste and excess fluid. The page identifies high blood pressure as a common cause of chronic kidney disease. query: Which intermediate biological processes might connect longstanding high blood pressure with chronic kidney disease?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- NIDDK states that hypertension can damage renal blood vessels and other components of the kidney filtering system. Damage to these structures can impair the kidneys' ability to remove waste and excess fluid. The page identifies high blood pressure as a common cause of chronic kidney disease. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0049; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK explains that high blood pressure can narrow and damage renal blood vessels and reduce blood flow. Damaged renal vessels may no longer function properly, impairing the kidneys' ability to remove waste and excess fluid. The article also identifies hypertension as a cause of kidney disease and describes progressive damage that can lead to kidney failure. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0048; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/high-blood-pressure]
- Persistent or uncontrolled high blood pressure can damage arterial walls over time. NHLBI explicitly describes hypertension-related arterial wall damage and identifies stroke and atherosclerosis among the serious complications of uncontrolled high blood pressure. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0028; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-pressure/symptoms]
- NIDDK defines diabetic kidney disease as kidney disease caused by diabetes. It explains that high glucose can damage renal blood vessels and impair their function, while kidney damage can reduce filtration of blood and allow waste to accumulate. Together these passages support renal vascular injury as a contributor to diabetic kidney dysfunction. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0039; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/preventing-problems/diabetic-kidney-disease]

query: What evidence supports or contradicts a proposed pathway from atrial fibrillation through clot formation to ischemic stroke?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- NHLBI explains that ischemic stroke can occur when a blood clot blocks cerebral blood flow. A clot traveling from elsewhere in the body is classified as an embolism. The page identifies atrial fibrillation among conditions associated with stroke-producing blood clots. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0053; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/stroke/causes]
- The American Heart Association explicitly explains that a clot formed in the atria may be carried from the heart to the brain, obstruct a cerebral artery and cause an embolic stroke, a subtype of ischemic stroke. This establishes embolization and cerebral arterial obstruction as the required additional events connecting an atrial thrombus with cardioembolic ischemic stroke. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0052; https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/atrial-fibrillation/why-atrial-fibrillation-af-or-afib-matters]
- NHLBI describes arterial blockage by a clot as a mechanism for ischemic stroke. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0002; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/stroke/causes]
- NHLBI explains that atrial fibrillation can impair effective pumping and cause blood to pool inside the heart. Pooled blood can form abnormal intracardiac clots. This directly establishes atrial fibrillation as a contributor to intracardiac thrombus formation; the atrial location is explicitly confirmed by K054S01. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0050; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/atrial-fibrillation/living-with]
- The American Heart Association explains that irregular atrial contractions during atrial fibrillation can prevent complete emptying of blood from the atria. Blood may pool within the atria and form clots, increasing the likelihood of atrial thrombus formation. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0051; https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/atrial-fibrillation/why-atrial-fibrillation-af-or-afib-matters]

query: Could prior brain injury lead to structural changes and later seizure risk, and which links are supported?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- NINDS identifies traumatic brain injury and brain damage as possible causes of epilepsy. It explains that attempts by the brain to repair itself following head injury may create abnormal nerve connections capable of producing seizures. The source also discusses increased recurrence risk following seizures in people with prior structural brain problems. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0057; https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/epilepsy-and-seizures]
- The Epilepsy Foundation explains that TBI can cause cerebral contusions, hemorrhage, edema, diffuse axonal injury and brain scarring. These establish structural brain injury after trauma. The article also associates certain brain injuries with later seizures and epilepsy but does not explicitly establish the complete process of epileptogenic neural circuit remodeling. query: How do asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease differ in their common triggers and underlying mechanisms?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- NHLBI explains that inhaled substances such as pollen and mold can provoke a strong immune response in some people, producing airway inflammation. It also identifies indoor and outdoor allergens as common triggers of asthma symptoms. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0041; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/asthma/causes]
- NHLBI identifies cigarette smoking as the most common cause of COPD in the United States. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0010; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/copd/causes]
- Wechsler and Wells describe cigarette smoke exposure as an inflammatory trigger in COPD. Chronic smoking increases oxidative stress, which contributes to lung inflammation. Smoke-related epithelial signaling releases cytokines and chemokines that recruit inflammatory cells, including neutrophils and macrophages, sustaining airway inflammatory responses. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0044; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11417604/]
- NHLBI directly explains that asthma flare-ups occur when airway swelling or tightening narrows the airways and makes breathing more difficult. Symptoms become substantially worse during attacks and may include coughing, chest tightness, wheezing and breathing difficulty. Inflammatory airway swelling is therefore a contributing mechanism of asthma exacerbations. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0043; https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/asthma/attacks]

query: How does the relationship between diabetes and chronic kidney disease compare with that between hypertension and kidney disease?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- NIDDK directly states that elevated blood glucose can damage kidney filters. Progressive kidney damage can impair the removal of waste and excess fluid from blood and may allow proteins to leak into urine. Kidney disease caused by diabetes is identified as diabetic kidney disease. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0040; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK defines diabetic kidney disease as kidney disease caused by diabetes. It explains that high glucose can damage renal blood vessels and impair their function, while kidney damage can reduce filtration of blood and allow waste to accumulate. Together these passages support renal vascular injury as a contributor to diabetic kidney dysfunction. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0039; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/preventing-problems/diabetic-kidney-disease]
- NIDDK identifies hypertension as a common adult CKD cause and describes damage to kidney blood vessels and filtering structures. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0013; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK identifies diabetes as a common cause of CKD in adults and describes kidney filter damage from elevated blood glucose. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0012; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]

query: How do hypertension and diabetes relate to risk of chronic kidney disease?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- NIDDK explicitly states that high blood glucose can damage blood vessels in the kidneys and that damaged vessels do not function as well. Longer diabetes duration and elevated blood glucose increase the likelihood of kidney damage. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0038; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/preventing-problems/diabetic-kidney-disease]
- NIDDK directly states that elevated blood glucose can damage kidney filters. Progressive kidney damage can impair the removal of waste and excess fluid from blood and may allow proteins to leak into urine. Kidney disease caused by diabetes is identified as diabetic kidney disease. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0040; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK identifies hypertension as a common adult CKD cause and describes damage to kidney blood vessels and filtering structures. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0013; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK states that hypertension can damage renal blood vessels and other components of the kidney filtering system. Damage to these structures can impair the kidneys' ability to remove waste and excess fluid. The page identifies high blood pressure as a common cause of chronic kidney disease. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0049; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK identifies diabetes as a common cause of CKD in adults and describes kidney filter damage from elevated blood glucose. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0012; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]

query: Which social or biological factors are associated with depression risk, and what causal claims are justified?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- MedlinePlus describes trauma and stressful life events as factors that may raise risk for depression. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0020; https://medlineplus.gov/depression.html]
- Alvaro et al. reviewed nine independent studies, including eight longitudinal studies, examining sleep disturbances and depression or anxiety. Several studies found that insomnia or sleep problems predicted later depression or higher depression levels, while other analyses identified reverse or bidirectional relationships. The review supports a longitudinal association between insomnia or sleep disruption and later depressive outcomes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0068; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3669059/]
- Li et al. synthesized 34 prospective cohort studies involving 172077 participants and reported an increased risk of subsequent depression among individuals with insomnia. The pooled relative risk was 2.27 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.89 to 2.71. Eligible depression outcomes included self-reported depressive symptom scales, clinician diagnoses and structured diagnostic interviews. These findings establish insomnia as a prospective predictor of subsequent depressive outcomes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0069; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27816065/]

query: How do hypertension-related and diabetes-related kidney disease mechanisms differ?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- NIDDK explicitly states that high blood glucose can damage blood vessels in the kidneys and that damaged vessels do not function as well. Longer diabetes duration and elevated blood glucose increase the likelihood of kidney damage. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0038; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/preventing-problems/diabetic-kidney-disease]
- NIDDK directly states that elevated blood glucose can damage kidney filters. Progressive kidney damage can impair the removal of waste and excess fluid from blood and may allow proteins to leak into urine. Kidney disease caused by diabetes is identified as diabetic kidney disease. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0040; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK identifies diabetes as a common cause of CKD in adults and describes kidney filter damage from elevated blood glucose. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0012; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK defines diabetic kidney disease as kidney disease caused by diabetes. It explains that high glucose can damage renal blood vessels and impair their function, while kidney damage can reduce filtration of blood and allow waste to accumulate. Together these passages support renal vascular injury as a contributor to diabetic kidney dysfunction. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0039; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/preventing-problems/diabetic-kidney-disease]
- NIDDK states that hypertension can damage renal blood vessels and other components of the kidney filtering system. Damage to these structures can impair the kidneys' ability to remove waste and excess fluid. The page identifies high blood pressure as a common cause of chronic kidney disease. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0049; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
These are source-attributed findings for the compared topics; no unsupported relative ranking is inferred.

Which risk factors for type 2 diabetes can change, and which should not be called direct causes?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- NIDDK states that type 2 diabetes develops when the body has difficulty using insulin and the pancreas does not make enough insulin to maintain glucose balance. Insulin resistance contributes to hyperglycemia and type 2 diabetes in the context of inadequate insulin secretion. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0036; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes]
- NIDDK includes family history in its list of type 2 diabetes risk factors. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0007; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/risk-factors-type-2-diabetes]
- NIDDK lists limited physical activity among reported risk factors for type 2 diabetes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0006; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/risk-factors-type-2-diabetes]
- NIDDK lists overweight or obesity among circumstances associated with higher likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0005; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/risk-factors-type-2-diabetes]
- Endotext describes insulin resistance in liver and muscle as an important pathogenic feature of type 2 diabetes; compensatory beta-cell secretion can initially maintain normal glucose, whereas inadequate beta-cell compensation permits hyperglycemia and progression to overt diabetes. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0037; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279115/]

query: What factors raise chronic kidney disease risk, and what evidence would distinguish association from causation?
final_response:
Based on the available source-attributed candidate evidence (not independently clinically verified):
- NIDDK states that hypertension can damage renal blood vessels and other components of the kidney filtering system. Damage to these structures can impair the kidneys' ability to remove waste and excess fluid. The page identifies high blood pressure as a common cause of chronic kidney disease. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0049; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK identifies diabetes as a common cause of CKD in adults and describes kidney filter damage from elevated blood glucose. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0012; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
- NIDDK identifies hypertension as a common adult CKD cause and describes damage to kidney blood vessels and filtering structures. [Evidence: PHASE2_CAND_0013; https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/causes]
